title: FOIA Request — RFP #23.09 Strategic Plan Facilitator: proposals, evaluation scores and contract

communications.subject: Michigan Freedom of Information Act Request: FOIA Request — RFP #23.09 Strategic Plan Facilitator: proposals, evaluation scores and contract
communications.communication:
Pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act, I hereby request the following records:

Under the Michigan Freedom of Information Act (MCL 15.231 et seq.), I request copies of the following records relating to Rochester Community Schools RFP #23.09, "Strategic Plan Facilitator" (2023; awarded to G&D Associates). The date range for this request is January 1, 2023 through September 30, 2026.

In this request, a reference to any record includes that record under any title the District uses for it; where a title differs, I request the record that serves that function.

1. The complete solicitation document for RFP #23.09, including all addenda and the evaluation criteria and weights.
2. The tabulation or summary of all proposals received (also called a bid abstract or proposal register), showing all proposers and all proposed prices, in its native spreadsheet format if maintained as one.
3. All evaluation and scoring records, including scoring sheets (also called evaluation forms, rating sheets, or scorecards), individual and consensus scores, rubrics, evaluator comments and worksheets (also called committee notes), and any interview or presentation scores. This includes evaluation records maintained in any e-procurement or agenda-management system the District uses.
4. All proposals submitted in response to RFP #23.09, including technical and cost proposals. If the volume is large, I prioritize: (a) the proposal of G&D Associates, and (b) the proposal of FourPoint Education Partners.
5. The executed contract (also called the agreement or professional services agreement) with G&D Associates, including scope of work, final price, term, and renewal options, plus all amendments, change orders, and extensions.
6. The board agenda item and supporting materials approving this award, including the funding source.
7. Line-item invoices submitted by, and payments (also called payment records or disbursement records) made to, G&D Associates under this contract, from the contract start through September 30, 2026.
8. The final deliverable(s) (also called work products or final reports) produced under this contract, including the adopted strategic plan document.

Please provide records in electronic format (searchable PDF or native files) where available, and produce records on a rolling basis as they are located and reviewed, beginning with the tabulation, scoring records, and executed contract, rather than holding all records until the full set is complete. If a responsive record is held by a third-party portal or vendor on the District's behalf, please produce it or identify where it is publicly posted. If any portion is withheld or redacted, please cite the specific statutory exemption and release all reasonably segregable portions. Pursuant to MCL 15.234, please provide an itemized fee estimate if fees will exceed $50, and contact me before processing if fees are expected to exceed $50; I do not authorize fees above $50 without my prior written approval.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 20 business days, as the statute requires.

Sincerely,

Felipe Acano

communications.subject: Washington Public Records Act Request: All Emails Sent to or Received from mcminimeelaw.com
communications.communication:
To Whom It May Concern:

Pursuant to the Washington Public Records Act, I hereby request the following records:

All electronic mail sent to or received from any email address operating under 
the domain "mcminimeelaw.com" (matching the wildcard string *@mcminimeelaw.com), 
exchanged with any Clover Park School District email account, alias, or internal 
routing node, acting as either the author, sender, primary recipient, 
carbon copy (CC), or blind carbon copy (BCC) holder.

The chronological scope of this request spans the entirety of the District's 
available archival retention window.



TECHNICAL PRE-EXCLUSION OF REPETITIVE SYSTEM DATA:

To maximize administrative processing efficiency, accelerate delivery, and 
eliminate unnecessary review burdens, the requester explicitly waives 
interest in, pre-excludes, and requests the system-level filtering out of 
the following non-substantive records categories:

1. Automated calendar invitations, change notifications, or updates.
2. Automated out-of-office or vacation autoreplies generated by either domain.
3. System-generated IT alerts, ticket confirmations, or password actions.



LIMITATION OF SCOPE & PRE-EXCLUSION OF SENSITIVE DATA:

The requester explicitly pre-excludes and waives any interest in the 
Personally Identifiable Information (PII) of any individual student under FERPA.

Pursuant to RCW 42.56.210, if the District asserts that specific internal 
staff names or student indicators are exempt from disclosure, the District is 
required to apply narrow blackouts exclusively to those individual text strings 
while releasing the remaining non-exempt text blocks, financial totals, 
and generalized policy or administrative discussions. 

Blanket withholding of entire records based on broad assertions of privilege 
or exempt status is explicitly contested; only the minimal exempt portions 
may be withheld.



MANDATORY STATUTORY COMPLIANCE TIMELINE:

As provided by RCW 42.56.520, a formal response is required within five (5) 
business days.

The requested documents will be made available to the general public, and this request is not being made for commercial purposes.

In the event that there are fees, I would be grateful if you would inform me of the total charges in advance of fulfilling my request. I would prefer the request filled electronically, by e-mail attachment if available or CD-ROM if not.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 5 business days, as the statute requires.

Sincerely,

Public Interest Mainstreaming Parenting

title: DEA Records Concerning Electric Daisy Carnival (EDC) Credentials, Access, and Federal Participation

communications.subject: Freedom of Information Act Request: DEA Records Concerning Electric Daisy Carnival (EDC) Credentials, Access, and Federal Participation
communications.communication:
To Whom It May Concern:

Pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act, I hereby request the following records:

Pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. § 552, I request the following records maintained by the Drug Enforcement Administration concerning Electric Daisy Carnival (EDC) events held at the Las Vegas Motor Speedway from January 1, 2023, through the date searches are conducted.

Specifically, I request:

Records reflecting the purchase, reimbursement, issuance, distribution, receipt, use, or acquisition of EDC admission credentials, tickets, VIP passes, hospitality credentials, media credentials, artist credentials, parking passes, backstage passes, or other event access credentials by or for DEA personnel.
Records reflecting requests made by DEA personnel to event organizers, promoters, contractors, or security providers for admission credentials, law-enforcement credentials, operational access, backstage access, VIP access, parking privileges, or other forms of event access.

Procurement records, purchase card records, reimbursement requests, travel vouchers, expense reports, invoices, receipts, or financial records relating to EDC admission credentials or event access.
Communications between DEA personnel and representatives of EDC, including but not limited to representatives of Insomniac Events, concerning credentials, operational access, law-enforcement support, intelligence gathering, interdiction activities, staffing, security coordination, or event participation.

Records sufficient to identify the number of DEA personnel assigned, deployed, credentialed, or granted access to EDC for each event year requested.

Calendars, briefing materials, meeting invitations, operational summaries, after-action reports, and executive briefings discussing DEA participation in EDC.

Communications between DEA Headquarters, the Los Angeles Field Division, and the Las Vegas District Office concerning EDC planning, staffing, credential requests, expenditures, intelligence support, or operational activities.

Records sufficient to identify overtime expenditures, travel expenditures, lodging expenditures, per diem payments, procurement expenditures, or other federal resources committed to EDC-related operations.

Any memoranda of understanding, operational agreements, coordination plans, or similar records concerning DEA participation in EDC-related activities.

Records sufficient to identify whether DEA personnel attended EDC in an official capacity, whether operational or observational, and the purpose of such attendance.

This request is not intended to seek information concerning private attendees or individual ticket purchasers. Rather, it seeks records concerning government operations, expenditures, staffing, access, and participation by DEA personnel.

For any records withheld in whole or in part, please provide a Vaughn index describing the basis for each withholding and release all reasonably segregable non-exempt portions.

Searches should include, at a minimum, DEA Headquarters, the Los Angeles Field Division, the Las Vegas District Office, email systems, Microsoft Teams communications, shared drives, calendars, expense systems, procurement systems, briefing repositories, and operational files reasonably likely to contain responsive records.

Fee Waiver Request

I request a waiver of all search, review, and duplication fees because disclosure of the requested information is in the public interest and is likely to contribute significantly to public understanding of federal law-enforcement activities and expenditures at one of the largest music festivals in the United States. The requested records concern government operations and the use of public resources and are not sought for commercial purposes.

The information obtained will be analyzed and disseminated to the public through open-government and news-reporting activities.

If fees are expected to exceed $25, please notify me before processing.

I request the records in electronic format whenever possible.

Respectfully,

William Fernandes

The requested documents will be made available to the general public, and this request is not being made for commercial purposes.

In the event that there are fees, I would be grateful if you would inform me of the total charges in advance of fulfilling my request. I would prefer the request filled electronically, by e-mail attachment if available or CD-ROM if not.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 20 business days, as the statute requires.

Sincerely,

William Fernandes

communications.subject: RE: Freedom of Information Act Request #26-06467-F
communications.communication:
U.S. DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
OFFICE OF INFORMATION POLICY
441 G Street, NW, 6th Floor
Washington, D.C. 20530
FREEDOM OF INFORMATION ACT ADMINISTRATIVE APPEAL
Appellant: William Fernandes
Agency: Drug Enforcement Administration
DEA FOIA Request No.: 25-07867-F

ADMINISTRATIVE APPEAL
To the Director:
Pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. § 552, and the Department of Justice implementing regulations, Appellant respectfully submits this Administrative Appeal requesting reversal or remand of the Drug Enforcement Administration's determination.
This appeal concerns whether DEA has satisfied its statutory burden of conducting a search reasonably calculated to locate all responsive records and whether the administrative record demonstrates compliance with the Department's legal and ethical obligations in administering the Freedom of Information Act.
I. INTRODUCTION
Congress enacted the Freedom of Information Act to promote transparency, accountability, and public confidence in Government.
The Department of Justice has adopted the Standards of Ethical Conduct applicable to its employees, including the obligation that employees "shall put forth honest effort in the performance of their duties" and "shall endeavor to avoid any actions creating the appearance that they are violating the law or the ethical standards set forth in this part." 5 C.F.R. § 2635.101(b)(5) & (14).
Those principles are particularly important in the administration of FOIA because requesters, reviewing authorities, and ultimately the public must necessarily rely upon the accuracy and completeness of agency representations describing searches performed outside public view.
II. BACKGROUND
The subject of this request concerns Electric Daisy Carnival ("EDC"), one of the largest and longest-running electronic music festivals in the United States. Having existed for more than thirty years and attracting hundreds of thousands of attendees annually, EDC has generated substantial law enforcement interest and interagency coordination over many years.
Given the event's longevity, national prominence, and recurring operational significance, it is reasonable to expect that responsive records have accumulated throughout numerous DEA offices, custodians, intelligence products, operational files, correspondence, planning documents, after-action reports, archived records, electronic communications, and historical record systems.
The longevity and prominence of the subject substantially increase the likelihood that responsive records exist in multiple repositories, making a narrowly focused search insufficient to satisfy the requirements of 5 U.S.C. § 552.
III. THIS APPEAL CONCERNS A RECURRING ADMINISTRATIVE DEFICIENCY
The administrative record in this matter cannot reasonably be viewed in isolation.
Appellant's experience with this DEA FOIA office over numerous requests and administrative appeals reflects a recurring pattern in which initial determinations have required appellate intervention before the agency fulfilled its statutory obligations. The purpose of review by the Office of Information Policy is not merely to correct isolated administrative mistakes, but to identify recurring deficiencies that undermine public confidence in the Department's administration of the Freedom of Information Act.
Where repeated remands become necessary before an agency performs searches reasonably calculated to locate responsive records, OIP should determine whether the issue extends beyond an individual request and reflects broader deficiencies in search methodology, supervisory review, quality control, training, or compliance with Department policy.
This appeal therefore requests not only review of the present determination but careful examination of whether the administrative practices employed by this FOIA office continue to satisfy the standards expected by the Department of Justice.

IV. THE FBI'S RESPONSIVE RECORDS FURTHER HIGHLIGHT THE NEED FOR REVIEW
Appellant submitted a substantially similar request to the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The FBI has advised Appellant that it identified responsive records FOIA Number: 1671779-000 and is presently processing those records for release.
Appellant fully recognizes that different Department of Justice components maintain different records.
However, when one DOJ component identifies a body of responsive records concerning substantially similar subject matter while another component reports dramatically different results, the disparity warrants careful administrative scrutiny.
This comparison does not establish that DEA necessarily possesses identical records.
It does, however, raise legitimate questions concerning whether DEA searched every office, custodian, archive, repository, and electronic records system reasonably likely to contain responsive information.
V. POLLING REQUESTS ARE AN IMPORTANT ACCOUNTABILITY MECHANISM
Appellant routinely submits corresponding requests to multiple agencies and Department components addressing the same factual subject.
These parallel requests serve an important oversight function.
Comparison of agency responses frequently identifies:
omitted custodians;
incomplete search methodologies;
overlooked repositories;
inconsistent interpretations of identical requests;
failures to refer records;
administrative deficiencies requiring corrective action.
Such requests strengthen—not burden—the administration of FOIA by allowing independent comparison of agency search efforts.
Indeed, Appellant's prior administrative appeals involving DEA have resulted in remands requiring additional processing after OIP determined that further administrative action was warranted. Those prior remands demonstrate the continuing importance of meaningful appellate review where legitimate questions exist concerning the adequacy of an agency's search.
VI. DEA HAS NOT MET ITS BURDEN
DEA bears the burden of demonstrating that it conducted a search reasonably calculated to locate all responsive records.
The present administrative record does not establish whether DEA searched:
Microsoft Outlook email;
Microsoft Teams communications;
archived mailboxes;
text messages;
government-issued mobile devices;
intelligence repositories;
shared drives;
historical archives;
supervisory correspondence;
operational planning files;
after-action reports;
legacy record systems;
referrals received from other Department of Justice components.
Absent such information, neither Appellant nor OIP can meaningfully evaluate whether DEA has discharged its statutory obligations.
VII. DUTY OF CANDOR
The Freedom of Information Act depends upon accurate factual representations regarding agency search efforts.
This appeal does not merely challenge DEA's conclusions.
It challenges whether the administrative record sufficiently demonstrates that DEA exercised the diligence required by law.
When significant questions remain concerning the scope of a search, the custodians contacted, the repositories examined, or the methodology employed, independent appellate review becomes essential to preserving confidence in the Department's FOIA process.
VIII. THE DEPARTMENT'S OWN ETHICAL STANDARDS SUPPORT REMAND
The Department of Justice requires its employees to conduct themselves in a manner that preserves public confidence in Government.
Employees are required to put forth honest effort in the performance of their duties and to endeavor to avoid actions creating the appearance that they are violating the law or applicable ethical standards.
Those principles reinforce—not replace—the statutory requirements imposed by FOIA.
Where the administrative record leaves substantial unanswered questions concerning the adequacy of an agency's search, the Department's own ethical standards support independent review to ensure that statutory obligations have been fully satisfied.
IX. REQUEST FOR RELIEF
Appellant respectfully requests that the Office of Information Policy:
Reverse or remand DEA's determination.
Direct DEA to conduct a new search reasonably calculated to locate all responsive records.
Require DEA to identify every custodian, office, and repository searched.
Require DEA to disclose the search terms employed.
Require DEA to explain the substantial disparity between its search results and those identified by another Department of Justice component processing substantially similar subject matter.
Require DEA to submit a supplemental declaration describing its search methodology in reasonable detail.
Direct release of all reasonably segregable portions of responsive records.
Grant such additional relief as OIP deems just and appropriate under the Freedom of Information Act.
Respectfully submitted,
/s/
William Fernandes

Also note that the DEA office assigned the FOIA number 26-06467-F on June 14, 2026 use of -F is usually an obstruction or instant denial indicator to best of my knowledge.

communications.subject: RE: Freedom of Information Act Request #26-06467-F
communications.communication:
Sent via DOJ Portal 10/08/26 by William

October 8, 2026
Director
Office of Information Policy
U.S. Department of Justice
441 G Street, NW, Sixth Floor
Washington, DC 20530
RE: FORMAL REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION, SUPERVISORY REVIEW, AND CORRECTIVE ACTION
Administrative Appeal No. A-2026-01955
DEA FOIA Request No. 26-06467-F
OIP Determination Dated September 29, 2026
Subject: Improper Whole-Request Rejection, Failure to Consider Partial Processing, Unsubstantiated Search Burden, and Concerns Regarding Administrative Impartiality
Dear Director:
I formally challenge the September 29, 2026 determination issued by Rianna Barrett, Associate Chief, Administrative Appeals Staff, affirming the Drug Enforcement Administration's rejection of FOIA Request No. 26-06467-F concerning records associated with the Electric Daisy Carnival (EDC), DEA employee participation, and DEA operations connected with the event.
I request reconsideration of this determination, supervisory review of the agency's reasonable-description analysis, and corrective action to facilitate the identification, processing, and disclosure of responsive records.
The determination appears to adopt an unnecessarily expansive characterization of the administrative burden associated with my request while failing to meaningfully consider DEA's established organizational structure, readily identifiable geographic jurisdictions, limited operational groups, centralized records repositories, and the possibility of separately processing sufficiently described categories of information.
The handling of this matter also raises legitimate concerns regarding administrative professionalism, impartiality, and the unnecessary expenditure of requester and government resources in resolving issues that could be addressed through established FOIA processing procedures.
I. IMPROPER WHOLE-REQUEST REJECTION AND FAILURE TO CONSIDER PARTIAL PROCESSING
OIP affirmed DEA's determination that the request was insufficiently described under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(3)(A) and 28 C.F.R. § 16.3(b).
The determination suggests that DEA would be required to search thousands of employee email accounts or undertake extensive research to identify personnel who may have participated in EDC.
This explanation fails to meaningfully distinguish among the separate categories of information identified in the request.
Federal agencies routinely issue partial grants and partial denials under FOIA. The statute contemplates individualized disclosure determinations, including the release of reasonably segregable nonexempt information.
Although the reasonable-description requirement must be satisfied before an agency is obligated to conduct a search, sufficiently identifiable portions of a request should receive appropriate consideration even where other portions require clarification.
The question is whether DEA evaluated the separately identifiable records categories before determining that the entire request could not reasonably be processed.
The determination does not document such an evaluation.
Records concerning DEA operational activity at a specific public event may be maintained in entirely different systems from records identifying individual employees who attended an event in a personal capacity.
These differences matter.
A centralized event-operation file, task-force coordination memorandum, supervisory communication, or administrative authorization may be reasonably identifiable without establishing the identity of every DEA employee who attended the event.
I request that OIP reconsider its blanket affirmation and direct DEA to evaluate whether independently identifiable categories of responsive records may be processed.
II. DEA'S NATIONAL WORKFORCE SIZE IS NOT A REASONABLE SUBSTITUTE FOR IDENTIFYING APPROPRIATE RECORDS CUSTODIANS
OIP's determination relies upon a generalized assertion that DEA would need to search thousands of employee email accounts.
That premise appears disconnected from the agency's actual organizational structure and the geographically limited subject matter of the request.
DEA's former Administrator, Anne Milgram, described the agency as employing nearly 10,000 personnel in congressional testimony dated July 27, 2023.
Regardless of whether the agency's total present workforce is closer to 10,000 or 12,500 personnel, its nationwide staffing complement provides little meaningful information concerning the effort necessary to identify records associated with a particular event in Las Vegas.
The relevant inquiry concerns the organizational units reasonably likely to maintain responsive records.
DEA's January 26, 2026 announcement appointing Anthony Chrysanthis as Special Agent in Charge of the Los Angeles Field Division expressly identifies Nevada among the jurisdictions supervised by that division.
Las Vegas therefore falls within the established regional organizational structure of DEA's Los Angeles Field Division.
This information is publicly available on DEA's own website.
It provides an identifiable starting point for determining which organizational units may maintain records associated with the requested activities.
Rather than presuming that thousands of unrelated individual employee accounts require examination, DEA could assess whether responsive records are maintained by:
1.	The DEA Las Vegas office and its relevant supervisory personnel.
2.	The Los Angeles Field Division and appropriate regional management offices.
3.	Any DEA operational group or task force assigned responsibilities associated with EDC.
4.	Personnel responsible for interagency event coordination or operational planning.
5.	Centralized operational, administrative, or correspondence systems reasonably likely to contain event-related records.
6.	Any designated operational coordinator, group supervisor, or administrative office responsible for maintaining activity records.
These are potential search locations requiring agency evaluation. Their identification does not presume that responsive records necessarily exist.
Nevertheless, the existence of DEA's established geographic hierarchy materially undermines an unexplained assertion that the request necessarily requires an agency-wide examination of individual employee accounts.
III. LIMITED TASK-FORCE STAFFING AND THE POSSIBILITY OF A NARROWLY TARGETED SEARCH
The agency's characterization also overlooks the possibility that any relevant operational activity associated with EDC would have been coordinated through a comparatively small group of personnel.
A geographically limited DEA operational group or task force might involve fewer than 100 personnel, potentially substantially fewer.
This figure is offered as an estimate for purposes of evaluating search methodology. DEA possesses the staffing, assignment, and organizational information necessary to establish the actual complement of any relevant unit.
The reasonable-description analysis should consider whether records could be identified through a limited number of supervisory or operational custodians rather than thousands of unrelated employees.
For example, a particular operational assignment might generate administrative communications, coordination records, reports, approvals, or activity documentation maintained within the responsible unit.
Such records would not necessarily require individual examination of every employee's email account.
OIP has not explained whether the Las Vegas office, the Los Angeles Field Division, or any potentially relevant task-force component was consulted regarding the existence or organization of responsive records.
Nor has OIP explained whether DEA attempted to identify the appropriate organizational component before concluding that a reasonable search could not be conducted.
I request reconsideration based upon a meaningful assessment of the actual administrative structures through which responsive records might be located.
IV. FAILURE TO ADEQUATELY APPLY 28 C.F.R. § 16.3(b)
DOJ's regulation at 28 C.F.R. § 16.3(b) provides the governing standard for reasonably describing requested records.
The regulation requires a description sufficient to enable agency personnel to locate records with a reasonable amount of effort.
Where an agency determines that a request does not reasonably describe the records sought, the regulation requires the agency to inform the requester what additional information is needed or explain why the request is otherwise insufficient.
The regulation also provides for assistance through agency FOIA personnel, the FOIA Public Liaison, and OIP.
OIP's September 29 determination affirms DEA's position and refers me to the DEA FOIA Public Liaison.
However, the determination does not meaningfully explain why DEA could not assess the readily identifiable regional and operational records repositories before concluding that the request was insufficiently described in its entirety.
An appropriate reasonable-description assessment should reflect the agency's actual records-management practices.
If DEA requires a particular date range, record category, custodian designation, organizational unit, or other identifying information, it should state precisely what is necessary.
A generalized characterization of the request as broad or sweeping does not explain whether sufficiently described portions can be processed.
I request that OIP direct DEA to identify the specific deficiencies associated with each disputed records category and provide actionable clarification requirements.
V. DOJ'S OWN PUBLISHED GUIDANCE FAVORS FAIR INTERPRETATION OF REQUESTS
OIP's published guidance, "Determining the Scope of a FOIA Request," emphasizes the importance of fairly interpreting the language of FOIA requests and avoiding unnecessarily restrictive constructions.
The guidance discusses Hemenway v. Hughes, 601 F. Supp. 1002, 1005 (D.D.C. 1985), and the importance of interpreting requests in a manner consistent with identifying responsive records.
The reasonable-description requirement serves a practical purpose: enabling agencies to locate records using reasonable effort.
It should not be administered through hypothetical search assumptions divorced from the agency's actual organization.
Federal agencies possess institutional knowledge regarding their records systems, supervisory assignments, filing practices, and organizational responsibilities that requesters generally cannot access.
This imbalance is particularly important where the requested information concerns internal law-enforcement operations or employee assignments.
DEA knows which components exercise jurisdiction over Las Vegas, which offices coordinate local activities, and which records systems are ordinarily used by those components.
A requester should not be required to identify every internal filing system or individual custodian before the agency meaningfully evaluates whether the requested records can reasonably be located.
I request that OIP apply its own published guidance in reviewing DEA's interpretation of the request.
VI. DISTINCTION BETWEEN REASONABLE SEARCH REQUIREMENTS AND EXHAUSTIVE INVESTIGATION
A FOIA search must be reasonably calculated to uncover responsive records. It does not ordinarily require an agency to examine every conceivable location or undertake unlimited investigative research.
That principle is relevant to DEA's burden analysis.
OIP's determination suggests that DEA would need to research which of its thousands of employees attended EDC.
That may describe one conceivable approach to an employee-participation inquiry.
It does not demonstrate that the same methodology would be necessary to identify operational records concerning the event.
A reasonable agency search may begin with the offices, custodians, or records systems most likely to contain the requested material.
DEA's identified regional structure offers practical opportunities for such an assessment.
The decision should explain why these more targeted approaches would not resolve at least portions of the request.
An assertion that an unnecessarily broad search would be burdensome does not independently establish that a narrower, organizationally appropriate search is unavailable.
VII. PARTIAL GRANTS, PARTIAL DENIALS, AND RECORDS SEGREGABILITY
FOIA permits different dispositions for separately identified categories of records.
An agency may release some responsive records, withhold others under applicable statutory exemptions, or determine that no records were located following an adequate search.
Under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(8), the agency must also consider applicable requirements concerning foreseeable harm and segregability when withholding responsive information.
These disclosure provisions do not eliminate the threshold reasonable-description requirement.
They nevertheless demonstrate that the statutory scheme recognizes differentiated treatment of records rather than unnecessarily categorical disposition.
OIP should evaluate whether the original submission included discrete, sufficiently described categories that could be processed without first resolving every issue concerning other categories.
For example, a request for operational coordination records may present materially different search considerations from a request requiring identification of all employees who personally attended a public event.
The two inquiries should not automatically be treated as administratively inseparable.
I request appropriate partial processing of any categories that independently satisfy FOIA's reasonable-description standard.
VIII. FAILURE TO ESTABLISH THE FACTUAL BASIS FOR THE CLAIMED SEARCH BURDEN
OIP's determination does not identify the factual or organizational basis for DEA's claim that thousands of email accounts would require examination.
It does not identify the components consulted, the categories of records reviewed for search feasibility, or the regional offices considered.
It provides no explanation of whether DEA evaluated centralized operational or supervisory records.
Nor does it establish that potentially responsive material could only be retrieved through individual employee-level searches.
I request that OIP obtain a substantive explanation addressing the following matters:
1.	Whether DEA consulted its Las Vegas office regarding the request.
2.	Whether the Los Angeles Field Division was consulted or identified as a potential records custodian.
3.	Whether any task-force, operational, or supervisory group was evaluated as a potential records repository.
4.	Whether records concerning event planning, operational authorization, coordination, or related administrative activities could be identified through centralized systems.
5.	The factual basis for asserting that thousands of employee accounts would require examination.
6.	Whether separately identifiable portions of the request were evaluated for partial processing.
7.	Whether DEA considered clarification of specific categories rather than wholesale rejection.
8.	Whether any responsive records had already been identified or located during preliminary processing.
A meaningful response to these questions would assist in determining whether the agency's original position reflected actual records-management limitations or an unnecessarily expansive construction of the requested search.
IX. ADMINISTRATIVE IMPARTIALITY, PROFESSIONALISM, AND APPEARANCE OF IMPROPRIETY
I have successfully pursued hundreds of federal Freedom of Information Act and Privacy Act requests, including complex administrative appeals involving multiple Department of Justice components.
My experience includes the evaluation of agency search methodologies, disclosure requirements, records-management systems, exemption determinations, and procedural deficiencies.
I am familiar with the practical limitations of FOIA administration and the distinction between reasonable records searches and unduly burdensome investigative inquiries.
Against that background, I find the September 29 determination unnecessarily dismissive of the substantive issues presented.
The agency's characterization of the request as requiring examination of thousands of employee accounts, followed by the suggestion that I contact the DEA FOIA Public Liaison, fails to adequately engage with readily identifiable organizational alternatives.
This handling creates an appearance of discouragement toward a requester who has consistently exercised established statutory disclosure rights.
I am concerned that the disposition may reasonably be perceived as intimidating, harassing, or unnecessarily adversarial, particularly where the asserted burden has not been explained through reference to DEA's actual organizational structure.
I request an objective supervisory examination of whether the handling of this appeal reflects appropriate standards of impartiality, fairness, and professional conduct.
An adverse determination alone does not establish intentional harassment or retaliation. The concern here is the combination of unsupported search assumptions, inadequate consideration of alternatives, and the resulting administrative burden placed upon the requester.
Federal employees entrusted with the administration of disclosure rights should endeavor to avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety.
They should also avoid unnecessary procedural obstacles that may discourage lawful participation in government transparency processes.
The Office of Information Policy occupies a particularly important position in maintaining these standards throughout the Department of Justice.
I request that OIP ensure its personnel approach administrative appeals with appropriate independence, professionalism, and an objective commitment to lawful disclosure.
X. UNNECESSARY EXPENDITURE OF REQUESTER AND GOVERNMENT RESOURCES
The handling of this matter raises additional concerns regarding administrative efficiency.
The preparation of an administrative appeal, followed by further reconsideration correspondence, requires substantial time, research, and effort.
These expenditures can often be avoided through reasonable communication concerning records scope and appropriate search locations.
A targeted inquiry to the DEA Las Vegas office or Los Angeles Field Division may require substantially fewer resources than an agency-wide inquiry involving thousands of employees.
Likewise, specific clarification regarding a disputed records category may eliminate unnecessary disagreement without requiring supervisory intervention or judicial proceedings.
The prolonged expenditure of public and private resources to resolve a dispute concerning readily identifiable geographic jurisdiction appears inconsistent with efficient FOIA administration.
I request that OIP endeavor to minimize unnecessary administrative friction and direct its attention toward resolving the underlying disclosure issues.
The purpose of the FOIA process is to facilitate lawful public access to agency records through established procedures.
Its effectiveness should be measured by the adequacy of those procedures and their results rather than by the number of administrative obstacles imposed upon requesters.
XI. REQUEST FOR SUPERVISORY REVIEW AND CORRECTIVE ACTION
I respectfully request the following corrective measures:
1.	Reconsider and withdraw the September 29, 2026 determination affirming DEA's rejection of FOIA Request No. 26-06467-F.
2.	Remand the request for renewed consideration under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(3)(A) and 28 C.F.R. § 16.3(b).
3.	Require DEA to evaluate separately identifiable categories of requested records and process any portions that independently satisfy the reasonable-description requirement.
4.	Direct DEA to consider a geographically limited assessment involving the Las Vegas office and Los Angeles Field Division.
5.	Require consideration of appropriate operational, supervisory, task-force, and centralized administrative records systems.
6.	Obtain the factual basis for DEA's assertion that thousands of employee email accounts would require examination.
7.	Require specific clarification instructions for any portion of the request that DEA continues to regard as insufficiently described.
8.	Facilitate the processing and disclosure of responsive records located through reasonable searches, with individualized application of any legally justified exemptions.
9.	Conduct a supervisory review of the handling of this appeal, including the adequacy of the written determination and any appearance of unnecessarily adversarial or discouraging treatment.
10.	Provide a written response addressing the objections presented and identifying the corrective action adopted.
11.	Ensure that the original request, administrative appeal, related correspondence, and processing records are retained in accordance with applicable federal records-management requirements.
XII. PRESERVATION OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND JUDICIAL RIGHTS
The September 29 determination advises that the administrative appeal has been denied and expressly identifies the right to seek judicial review under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(B).
This correspondence seeks discretionary reconsideration and supervisory review of that determination.
I preserve all applicable administrative and judicial rights and remedies, including judicial review and assistance through the Office of Government Information Services.
This request for reconsideration should be addressed on its merits without prejudicing any previously accrued right to judicial review.
I further request preservation of records documenting the handling of the underlying FOIA request and appeal, including internal communications, processing notes, referrals, consultations, and materials relied upon in reaching the reasonable-description determination, subject to applicable records-retention obligations.
XIII. CONCLUSION
The September 29 determination rests upon an insufficiently explained assertion that processing my request would require examining thousands of DEA employee accounts.
That proposition deserves substantial scrutiny given DEA's established organizational structure, the Los Angeles Field Division's jurisdiction over Nevada, and the existence of identifiable regional and operational offices through which potentially responsive records may be maintained.
DEA's nationwide workforce size cannot substitute for a practical assessment of the records systems reasonably likely to contain information relevant to a specific public event in Las Vegas.
A hypothetical nationwide search should not displace consideration of geographically limited and organizationally appropriate alternatives.
The reasonable-description requirement should be applied constructively, with due regard for the agency's actual records-management practices and the independently identifiable categories of information requested.
I further request that OIP ensure its administrative personnel exercise appropriate impartiality, professionalism, and sound judgment when corresponding with experienced FOIA requesters.
The unnecessary expenditure of time and resources in avoidable administrative disputes undermines both the purpose of the Freedom of Information Act and the public's confidence in government records administration.
I request prompt supervisory intervention, reconsideration of the September 29 determination, and appropriate corrective action to advance the processing and disclosure of responsive agency records.
Respectfully,
/s/
William Fernandes
________________________________________

communications.communication:
To Whom It May Concern:

Pursuant to the Washington Public Records Act, I hereby request the following records:

For the period from January 1, 2010 to the date this request was filed, please provide a spreadsheet of all complaints against officers in CSV or Excel format with only the following columns: Investigation/Complaint No., Incident Type, Occurred Date, Complaint Reported On Date, Employee Badge Number, Employee First Name, Employee Last Name, Allegation, Allegation: Policy/Directive Violated, Allegation: Finding, Disposition, Discipline Imposed.

Please provide all complaints, regardless of severity,in cluding any complaints that may not have been classified for full investigation and were referred to an employee's supervisor for counseling or retraining as well as complaints that were investigated by an employee's command instead of the normal internal affairs process. I would ask that you fulfill my request in a single installment in one spreadsheet instead of splitting it up into multiple annual spreadsheets if possible.

The requested documents will be made available to the general public, and this request is not being made for commercial purposes.

In the event that there are fees, I would be grateful if you would inform me of the total charges in advance of fulfilling my request. I would prefer the request filled electronically, by e-mail attachment if available or CD-ROM if not.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 5 business days, as the statute requires.

Sincerely,

Rose Terse

RE: Pierce County Sheriff PUBLIC RECORDS REQUEST of March 19, 2026, Reference # P043044-031926. 
August 06, 2026 
Dear Rose Terse, 
In accordance with the Public Records Act, RCW 42.56, this letter acknowledges receipt of your request for records dated 3/19/2026 7:47:07 PM and received by Pierce County Sheriff on 3/20/2026 8:30:00 AM.  Your request asks for the following: 
“To Whom It May Concern: 

Pursuant to the Washington Public Records Act, I hereby request the following records: 

For the period from January 1, 2010 to the date this request was filed, please provide a spreadsheet of all complaints against officers in CSV or Excel format with only the following columns: Investigation/Complaint No., Incident Type, Occurred Date, Complaint Reported On Date, Employee Badge Number, Employee First Name, Employee Last Name, Allegation, Allegation: Policy/Directive Violated, Allegation: Finding, Disposition, Discipline Imposed. 

Please provide all complaints, regardless of severity,in cluding any complaints that may not have been classified for full investigation and were referred to an employee's supervisor for counseling or retraining as well as complaints that were investigated by an employee's command instead of the normal internal affairs process. I would ask that you fulfill my request in a single installment in one spreadsheet instead of splitting it up into multiple annual spreadsheets if possible. 

The requested documents will be made available to the general public, and this request is not being made for commercial purposes. 

In the event that there are fees, I would be grateful if you would inform me of the total charges in advance of fulfilling my request. I would prefer the request filled electronically, by e-mail attachment if available or CD-ROM if not. 

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 5 business days, as the statute requires. 

Sincerely, 

Rose Terse 

Upload documents directly: https://www.muckrock.com/respond/2240777/” 

To date, we have released to you the following installments: 

Installment 2: 
2 Excels, 2 pdf files 

Date Produced: 8/6/2026 

Productions: 2 excel files, pages 5-73 

At this time, we are prepared to produce the next installment of records.  In this installment, 2 excel files and 69 pages numbered 5 through 73 were located and determined to be responsive to your request. Please log back into the “ ” within the portal to access all released records. Select this request and select "View Files". My Request Center 

Please see the corresponding exemption log for additional information regarding any redactions and exemptions that apply to these records. 

Pursuant to RCW 42.56.120(4) and Pierce County Code 2.04.040(H) if you do not inspect or retrieve these records made available to you through the County web portal or file transfer protocol service within 30 calendar days after receiving this notice of the availability of the records, this agency may stop providing further installments of records and close out the request. 

It will take additional time for us to review all the files that may contain records responsive to your request and to determine which records or portions of records, if any, are exempt pursuant to law. Accordingly, we estimate that we will be providing the next installment of records to you on or before Thursday, October 1, 2026. 

I will notify you if records are available sooner, more time is required to complete the search for responsive records, or if additional clarifying information is needed from you.  If you have any questions, believe we have somehow misunderstood your request(s) or wish to clarify your request, please do not hesitate to contact me.  To respond via the , open this request “Details” page and send a “New Message”. Public Records Portal 

Sincerely, 
Christina Smith 
Public Records Officer 
Pierce County Sheriff

title: Jail booking fields and 30-day booking log (Chaffee County Sheriff)

communications.subject: Colorado Open Records Act Request: Jail booking fields and 30-day booking log (Chaffee County Sheriff)
communications.communication:
Hello, and thank you for the work you do at the Chaffee County Sheriff.

I'm writing from the Records Desk at Tempo by Multido with a small public records request under the Colorado Open Records Act (CORA) and Colorado Criminal Justice Records Act (CCJRA). I know records staff are busy, so I've tried to keep this as simple as I can.

Could you please share:

1. A list of the fields your jail booking system keeps (for example: booking number, booking date, name, date of birth, charges, bond, release date, booking photo). A screenshot, a report header or a short description is perfectly fine.
2. The booking log for the most recent 30 days, in whatever electronic form is easiest for you. A standard report export, a spreadsheet or a PDF all work.

I'd also love to know: does your office offer an email list, notification system or regular report (daily or weekly) that shares new bookings or arrests? If so, we'd be glad to sign up, so you wouldn't need to handle requests like this one in the future.

If any part is exempt, please feel free to send the rest. And if another office is the better place to ask, a quick pointer would be very much appreciated.

Thank you so much for your time and help. We really appreciate it.

Warmly,
Logan
